title: Self-healing concrete for infrastructure lifespan
bottleneck: Concrete cracks inevitably, letting water and chlorides reach rebar and start corrosion — the main killer of bridges and marine structures. Self-healing approaches using bacteria, encapsulated polymers, or expansive minerals can seal small cracks in the lab, but healing is slow, limited to sub-millimeter cracks, and unproven over decades of freeze-thaw and loading. No method yet guarantees healing across the crack sizes that actually cause failure.
why_it_blocks: Infrastructure replacement is enormously carbon- and capital-intensive; doubling concrete lifespan would slash both. Without reliable self-healing, structures keep failing on 50-year cycles and the repair backlog grows faster than budgets.
current_state: Bacterial self-healing concrete has been used in small real-world pours with encouraging early results. But the gap between sealing hairline lab cracks and autonomously repairing structural-scale damage in service remains wide.
